# Second Brain OS: full text

> A guide to building a knowledge base your AI agent maintains, in plain markdown you own, plus an agents course and handbooks.

The markdown of all 132 pages, in reading order, each under a page header. Relative links inside a page point to files in the repository (https://github.com/kuuratsanik/second-brain-os/tree/main/); the index is https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kuuratsanik/second-brain-os/main/llms.txt.

========================================================================
PAGE 1 of 132: What a second brain actually is
Section: Guide: Concepts
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kuuratsanik/second-brain-os/main/docs/01-concepts/what-is-a-second-brain.md
========================================================================

# What a second brain actually is

One local folder of plain text that an agent reads and writes, holding what you
have read and understood, that you can ask questions.

That is the whole definition. Everything else in this guide is detail about
making it work.

## What it is not

**Not a prettier notes app.** The point is not organisation. You can organise
notes beautifully and still never reopen them.

**Not a chatbot with your PDFs attached.** Attaching documents to a chat gets you
answers about those documents in that session. Nothing accumulates, nothing
connects, and next week you attach them again.

**Not a memory feature.** Assistants that remember facts about you are useful and
are a different thing. This is a body of knowledge you own, that outlives any
particular tool.

## The three jobs

**Capture.** Everything you read, watch and write down lands in one place with
near-zero friction. If capture takes effort, nothing else matters, because there
will be nothing to organise.

**Connect.** New material gets linked into what is already there. This is the job
humans stop doing after two weeks and the reason every previous note system
failed. It is also the entire value: unconnected notes are a folder.

**Answer.** You ask questions across everything at once, and get answers grounded
in your own sources with citations you can open.

## Where the value comes from

Not from any single page. A page is a slightly better version of a note you could
have written.

It comes from density. At fifty sources, the vault starts connecting things you
read months apart. At five hundred, it answers questions you could not have
answered yourself, because nobody holds five hundred sources in their head at
once.

That is why the first two weeks feel underwhelming and why most people quit
before the payoff. The system is not broken at thirty pages, it is just
early. See [what good looks like](what-good-looks-like.md) for a realistic
timeline.

## Next

[The save-for-later paradox](the-save-for-later-paradox.md)

========================================================================
PAGE 2 of 132: The save-for-later paradox
Section: Guide: Concepts
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kuuratsanik/second-brain-os/main/docs/01-concepts/the-save-for-later-paradox.md
========================================================================

# The save-for-later paradox

You screenshot the post. You bookmark the article. You save the video to a
playlist named "watch later" that has four hundred items in it.

You do not go back. Almost nobody does.

## Why saving fails

Saving feels like an action, and it discharges the feeling that made you want to
save. The intention gets spent at the moment of saving rather than at the moment
of reading, which is why the queue grows and the reading does not.

Then retrieval costs more than it is worth. Finding the thing you saved means
remembering that you saved it, remembering where, and searching wording you no
longer recall. Compared to a fresh search, the saved item loses, so you search
again and save again.

And the pile itself becomes a deterrent. Four hundred unread items is not a
resource, it is a debt you avoid looking at.

## What actually changes it

Not better tagging. Not a better read-later app. Not discipline, which is the
thing that already failed.

What changes it is removing the step you keep failing at. If the filing and
connecting happen without you, the queue stops being a queue: the material is
already processed, already linked, already reachable by asking a question in
plain language.

The retrieval cost inverts too. You no longer need to remember that you saved
something, or where. You ask what you know about a topic, and things you had
forgotten saving come back.

## The honest limit

The system does not make you read things. It processes what you feed it, and
what you feed it is still your choice.

What it does is make saving worth doing. That is a smaller claim than most
second-brain pitches make, and it is the one that holds up after a month.

[The LLM wiki pattern](llm-wiki-pattern.md)

========================================================================
PAGE 3 of 132: The LLM wiki pattern
Section: Guide: Concepts
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kuuratsanik/second-brain-os/main/docs/01-concepts/llm-wiki-pattern.md
========================================================================

# The LLM wiki pattern

The specific pattern this guide implements, published by Andrej Karpathy as a
[gist](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) on
2026-04-04.

The inversion in one sentence: instead of you maintaining notes and occasionally
asking an AI about them, the AI maintains the wiki and you read it.

## What the pattern specifies

**The wiki is primary.** Raw sources are an archive you keep and rarely open.
The wiki is what you and the agent both work from, written in plain language,
one idea per page, densely linked.

**Compilation, not summarization.** Each new source is integrated into existing
pages rather than added beside them as another summary. A page about a concept
improves as sources accumulate; it does not turn into a list of what each source
said.

**Three operations.** Ingest brings new material in. Query answers from the
wiki. Lint is a periodic health check of the wiki. The gist names these three;
everything else here is variation on them.

## Why it holds up

Because it removes the one task that killed every previous system. Linking fifty
notes to each other every time you read a paper is genuinely boring work that
humans stop doing, and the wiki dies when the maintainer gets tired.

The other reason is that it needs no infrastructure. Markdown files, wikilinks,
an agent that can read and write files. No database, no index to keep fresh, no
service to depend on.

## Where the gist stops

It describes intent, not implementation. Integrate new sources, lint
periodically, treat the wiki as primary. It suggests an `index.md` and a
`log.md` and a schema file such as `CLAUDE.md`, and calls all of it optional.

The mechanics are left open, which is why every implementation of it differs.
How integration handles contradictions, what a page must contain, when lint
runs, who the wiki is written for. This guide's answers to those are in
[Structuring](../04-structuring/README.md), and they are opinions, not the
pattern itself.

## What people build on top

The gist does not cover a project layer or scheduled automation. This guide adds
them: see [the two layers](two-layers.md) and [Agents](../06-agents/README.md).

The pattern also spread quickly because the primitives are ordinary: anyone with
an agent and a folder can run it, and the implementations are all readable
markdown. See [resources](../../resources/skills.md) for the ones worth reading.

## Next

[The two layers](two-layers.md)

========================================================================
PAGE 4 of 132: The two layers
Section: Guide: Concepts
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kuuratsanik/second-brain-os/main/docs/01-concepts/two-layers.md
========================================================================

# The two layers

Most second-brain setups fail because they pick one shape and try to make it do
two jobs.

**The knowledge layer** answers "what do I know about X". It is organised by
idea, it grows forever, and its value is in the links between pages. This is the
LLM wiki pattern: sources in, concepts out, everything connected.

**The project layer** answers "what am I doing this week". It is organised as a
pipeline, inputs to outputs, and most of it goes cold the moment the project
ships.

They fail differently when merged. A wiki with project folders in it fills up
with dead task lists that make every search worse. A project system with
conceptual notes in it buries the working files under material nobody opens
while working.

## How they connect

Projects consume the knowledge layer and feed it back:

```
        wiki/concepts ──────> project Inputs/
              ▲                      │
              │                      ▼
        ingest what                Process/ ──> Outputs/
        you learned                              │
              └──────────────────────────────────┘
```

Work produces material worth keeping. Ingesting your own finished work is the
step almost everyone skips, and it is the one that makes the second project in
a domain meaningfully faster than the first.

## Which to build first

The knowledge layer, if you read a lot and retain little.

The project layer, if your problem is that you re-explain your situation to a
chat window every morning.

Both eventually. See [vault structure](../02-setup/vault-structure.md) for the
layout that keeps them separate inside one folder.

PAGE 5 of 132: Why markdown and plain text
Section: Guide: Concepts
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kuuratsanik/second-brain-os/main/docs/01-concepts/why-markdown-and-plain-text.md
========================================================================

# Why markdown and plain text

The format looks like a detail. It decides whether the system works.

## Agents handle files better than APIs

An agent reading a folder does what it is best at: reading text and writing text.
No schema to learn, no API to call correctly, no failure mode where a request
half-succeeds.

That reliability compounds over thousands of operations. A pipeline that writes
markdown files fails in ways you can see in a diff; one that writes through an
API fails in ways you find out about later.

## Portability is not theoretical

Every previous notes tool people trusted either shut down, changed pricing, or
made export deliberately awkward.

Plain files remove the question. Your vault opens in any text editor, syncs with
any tool, and works with any agent that reads files. Switch models, switch
editors, switch operating systems, and the vault is unaffected because it was
never in anything.

This matters more than usual here, because a second brain accumulates value over
years. A format that traps you is a format that eventually costs you the whole
thing.

## Wikilinks as a graph format

`[[Page name]]` is a two-character convention that produces a real graph, is
readable as text, and survives every tool that does not understand it, because
in the worst case it is still just words in a sentence.

You can parse it with a regex, which is what `scripts/graph_export.py` does. Try
that with a proprietary block reference format.

## Git works on it

Text diffs. That single property is what makes an agent safe to run unattended:
every change it makes is reviewable, revertible, and attributable to a run.

Binary formats and database-backed apps give you no equivalent. You either trust
the automation completely or you do not automate.

## The limits

Plain text is bad at a few things, and pretending otherwise is how people end up
frustrated.

**Structured queries at scale.** Dataview covers a lot, but past a few thousand
pages, relational questions want a real database. Export the graph rather than
abandoning markdown; see [exporting the
graph](../05-graphs/exporting-your-graph.md).

**Rich media.** Images live beside the text as files, not in it. Diagrams are
attachments.

**Concurrent editing.** Two agents writing the same file conflict in the way
files conflict, which is to say badly.

None of those outweigh portability for a personal vault. All of them are worth
knowing before you hit them.

PAGE 6 of 132: Zettelkasten, PARA, evergreen notes
Section: Guide: Concepts
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kuuratsanik/second-brain-os/main/docs/01-concepts/pkm-lineage.md
========================================================================

# Zettelkasten, PARA, evergreen notes

None of this is new. The methods people abandoned were mostly right, and it is
worth knowing which parts of them still apply, because the good ideas came with a
cost that has now changed.

## Zettelkasten

Niklas Luhmann's slip-box, popularised for a modern audience by Sönke Ahrens in
"How to Take Smart Notes". Atomic notes, one idea each, densely cross-referenced,
written in your own words.

**Still right:** atomic notes, dense linking, rewriting in your own words rather
than clipping quotes. All three are in this guide's [structuring
rules](../04-structuring/README.md).

**The cost:** every link was manual. Reading one paper meant deciding where it
connected among hundreds of existing notes, which is real cognitive work and the
reason most slip-boxes die in month three.

## PARA

Tiago Forte's system from "Building a Second Brain": Projects, Areas, Resources,
Archive. Organise by actionability rather than by subject.

**Still right:** the insight that project material and reference material want
different structures. That is exactly [the two layers](two-layers.md), arrived at
from a different direction.

**The cost:** constant filing decisions, and the fact that actionability changes,
so the same note moves between categories over time.

## Evergreen notes

Andy Matuschak's approach: notes written to be reread and improved over years,
concept-oriented, densely linked, developed slowly.

**Still right:** the standard for what a good concept page is. Matuschak's
argument that notes should be written for your future self, not as a record of
having read something, is the bar this guide's concept pages aim at.

**The counterweight:** his position is that the writing is the thinking, and
delegating it means not doing the thinking. That is a real objection to this
whole approach and worth sitting with rather than dismissing.

## What changed

One thing: the maintenance is now delegable.

Every system above works. Every one of them failed for the same reason, which is
that they required a human to do boring linking work forever. An agent doing it
does not get tired in month three.

## What did not change

You still have to choose what to read. You still have to decide what matters.
The agent files and connects; it does not have taste, and a vault fed
indiscriminately is a well-organised pile.

And Matuschak's objection stands: understanding comes from writing. The way to
keep it is to write the concept pages that matter to you yourself, and let the
agent handle sources, entities and the linking. That split is a preference this
guide does not enforce, and it is worth deciding deliberately rather than by
default.

[Wiki vs RAG](wiki-vs-rag.md)

========================================================================
PAGE 7 of 132: Wiki vs RAG
Section: Guide: Concepts
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kuuratsanik/second-brain-os/main/docs/01-concepts/wiki-vs-rag.md
========================================================================

# Wiki vs RAG

The default advice for asking questions of your own documents is to embed them
in a vector database. This guide does something else, and the reason is
structural rather than a preference about tools.

## The two approaches

**RAG** stores your documents as chunks with embeddings. A question retrieves the
most similar chunks and the model answers from them. Nothing is written; the
corpus stays as it was.

**A wiki** processes documents once, into pages an agent wrote and linked.
Questions are answered by navigating those pages. The corpus is transformed and
keeps improving.

The difference is where the work happens. RAG does it at query time, every time,
from scratch. A wiki does it once, at ingest, and the result is reused.

## What that buys

**Understanding accumulates.** The tenth source about a topic improves the page
the first nine built. In RAG, the tenth document is just another chunk, and
nothing gets better as the corpus grows, only larger.

**Contradictions are visible.** Two documents disagreeing produce two chunks that
may never be retrieved together. On a page, the disagreement is written down,
dated, and unavoidable.

**Answers are checkable.** The page cites sources you can open. Retrieved chunks
are fragments without the reasoning that connected them.

**No infrastructure.** No index, no re-embedding, no drift between the store and
the files.

## What it costs

**Ingest is expensive.** Writing and linking pages costs model time up front,
where RAG's ingest is nearly free.

**Quality depends on the ingest.** A bad page contract produces a bad vault, and
you find out later. RAG's failures are at query time and are more visible.

**Recall depends on linking.** A page nobody linked is a page the graph cannot
reach. RAG will find it by similarity regardless.

## The honest position

This trade is right for a personal, curated corpus of a few thousand pages and
wrong for a million documents nobody organised.

Which is to say it is right for a second brain and wrong for a search product,
and most advice about RAG is written for the second case. See [adding RAG when
you need it](../07-retrieval/rag-on-top.md) for the threshold where the answer
flips, and [graph vs embeddings](../05-graphs/graph-vs-vectors.md) for the
retrieval mechanics.

PAGE 8 of 132: What good looks like

========================================================================

# What good looks like

Concrete criteria, so you can tell whether yours is working rather than guessing.

## The test

Ask it something you half-remember reading about, months ago, that you cannot
name precisely.

If it comes back with the idea, the sources, and two related things you had
forgotten, it works. If it returns nothing, or returns a general explanation that
could have come from any model, it does not.

## Signals of health

**You reach for it before searching the web.** The strongest signal, and it
happens on its own once the vault is dense enough.

**Answers cite pages you can open,** and the pages say what the answer said.

**The graph has clusters you did not plan.** Evidence it is tracking what you
actually pay attention to rather than what you told it to.

**New sources mostly update existing pages** rather than creating new ones. That
means the vault has the concepts already and is deepening rather than sprawling.

**It contradicts you occasionally,** because you have material on both sides of
something.

## Signals of trouble

**Orphan rate climbing.** Ingestion has stopped linking. See
[metrics](../05-graphs/metrics.md).

**Pages that read as summaries** rather than explanations. The page contract in
`CLAUDE.md` needs tightening.

**Concept pages untouched for months while sources keep arriving.** New material
is landing in new pages instead of updating existing ones, which produces four
pages about one thing.

**You stopped opening it.** The honest one. Usually means capture broke, not that
the idea failed.

## A realistic timeline

**Week one.** Setup, ten or twenty sources. Feels like a folder with extra steps.
This is normal and it is where most people quit.

**Week two to four.** Fifty to a hundred sources. First moment of the vault
connecting two things you read weeks apart. This is when it starts being worth
the setup.

**Month three.** A few hundred pages. It answers questions faster than you could
by rereading, and it surfaces things you had forgotten saving.

**Month six.** It knows things you do not remember learning. That is the state
everyone describes as the payoff, and it is real, and it takes six months of
feeding it.

PAGE 9 of 132: Obsidian and your first vault
Section: Guide: Setup
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kuuratsanik/second-brain-os/main/docs/02-setup/obsidian-install-and-vault.md
========================================================================

# Obsidian and your first vault

Obsidian is the storage half of the system. It is free to use (Obsidian's [help](https://help.obsidian.md/credit) says it "is completely free to use"), it keeps everything as
plain text files on your own machine, and it renders the links between notes as
a graph. Nothing here is stored in a company's cloud, and the files stay
readable in any text editor if you ever walk away from the app.

## Install

Download from [obsidian.md](https://obsidian.md) and install it.

If you ran the Quickstart from the [README](../../README.md), you already have
a `~/brain` folder with the starter structure in it. On the welcome screen,
click **Open folder as vault** and pick it.

If you are starting from nothing, click **Create new vault** instead. Name it
something short you will type often, `brain` works. Pick a folder on your
machine and click **Create**, then copy the contents of
[`vault-template/`](../../vault-template/) into it, including the hidden
`.gitignore`.

Either way, that folder is now your second brain. Everything the agent writes
lands there as markdown files.

The template is an opinionated starter, not a blank vault: it assumes an agent
that works without asking first, six domains and notes in more than one
language, and it ships with no personal facts. The [CLAUDE.md
interview](claude-md.md) fills in your profile. If you did not run the
Quickstart's git step, do it once now with the commands in the
[template README](../../vault-template/README.md): the vault has to be its own
git repository, not a folder inside another one, because the agent's rails
commit a checkpoint before any destructive step.

## Make one note by hand

Do this once before automating anything, so the mechanic is not abstract.

Click the new-note icon, type a sentence, then type `[[goals]]`. The bracketed
word becomes a link to a page called `goals`, whether or not that page exists
yet. Click it and Obsidian creates the page.

That is the entire data model: notes pointing at notes. Everything the agent
does later is this, at volume, without you doing it.

## Where to put the vault

Somewhere with a stable path you can type from a terminal. Avoid a folder your
cloud sync client rewrites aggressively, because an agent writing files while a
sync client rewrites them produces conflict copies that are genuinely painful
to untangle. See [git and sync](git-and-sync.md) for the options that work.

Avoid spaces in the folder name. You will be pasting this path into commands.

## Settings worth changing now

- **Files and links → New link format:** Relative path to file or Shortest path
  when possible, consistently (Obsidian's
  [settings reference](https://help.obsidian.md/settings) lists the options). Mixed link formats are a common cause of broken links
  after a rename.
- **Files and links → Automatically update internal links:** on.
- **Editor → Properties in document:** Visible (the default) or Source. You want
  to see the metadata the agent writes, at least for the first weeks.

[Claude Code in the vault](claude-code-setup.md)

PAGE 10 of 132: Claude Code in the vault
